Maladaptive Strategies.value: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being alone in a room or building
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette: Ahmed is a 52-year-old Middle Eastern man who has been widowed for several years. He was once an accomplished actor, but his life took a devastating turn when he witnessed the tragic death of his young daughter during a shooting at her school. The traumatic event left him with a profound sense of guilt and a deep-seated fear that haunts his daily life. Since the tragedy, Ahmed has been acutely sensitive to auditory triggers such as children crying or related sounds, which immediately transport him back to the day he lost his daughter. These triggers also surface when he encounters media coverage related to similar incidents. Each time these triggers occur, they evoke intense negative emotions and fragmented memories of that harrowing day. Ahmed's distress has led him to develop maladaptive strategies such as people-pleasing behaviors and a strong aversion to being alone or in crowded places. He often goes along with whatever others want to feel safe, even if it means compromising his own needs and desires. His fear of being alone intensifies when he is reminded of the event through auditory triggers, which makes him seek out company as a coping mechanism. The fragmented nature of his memories compounds his distress. When he remembers the event, the pieces do not fit together coherently, leading to intense guilt each time he recalls it. This photographic recall makes it difficult for him to feel safe or trust that he is truly out of danger, even when others reassure him otherwise. Ahmed's negative appraisals further exacerbate his symptoms. He feels that institutions and people who were supposed to protect them failed him, and the lack of accountability from those responsible adds to his sense of injustice. The guilt he carries for not being able to prevent what happened is overwhelming, leading him to doubt his own efficacy and worth. Over time, these triggers have reinforced his maladaptive strategies, creating a cycle that tightens with each encounter. His inability to concentrate and his deep-seated distrust in safety make it challenging for him to function normally. The fragmented memories of the event often surface when he is alone or in crowded places, leading him to avoid such situations altogether. Ahmed's people-pleasing behavior has strained his relationships, as he has difficulty asserting his own needs and boundaries. His work as an actor has suffered, with performances becoming increasingly difficult due to his concentration issues and heightened anxiety around auditory triggers. He often avoids auditions or rehearsals in crowded venues, further isolating himself from his craft. The negative appraisals of institutional failure and lack of accountability have also led Ahmed to question the broader systems that are supposed to provide safety and security. This constant vigilance has made it nearly impossible for him to feel truly secure, even in environments where others perceive no threat. The guilt he feels is a continuous source of self-doubt and fear. What finally brought Ahmed to seek help was a particularly intense episode triggered by media coverage of another school shooting. He realized that his avoidance behaviors were increasingly interfering with his ability to function and maintain meaningful relationships. He is most afraid that the memory will never leave him, but he also hopes for some relief from the guilt and fear that plague him daily. Ahmed's journey into therapy aims to break this cycle by addressing both his triggers and the underlying negative appraisals that have kept him trapped in a loop of distress. He seeks understanding and support to navigate through these overwhelming emotions and restore a sense of safety and self-worth.
